catalog_locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.8 'Stress', pp. 72-73; exceptions in secs. 3.3.1-3.3.2, pp. 57-58; compound stress also sec. 5.11.2, p. 188; dictionary key ('irregular stress' mark) in the dictionary front matter.
catalog_quote: Stress is indicated by a higher impressionistic intensity on the stressed vowel. Unstressed vowels are not reduced in any way; they are just not pronounced as prominently as the stressed syllable. Stress in single words almost always falls on the penultimate syllable; there are a few exceptions as detailed in §3.3.1 and §3.3.2. There is also a tendency for words where the final syllable contains a complex coda (i.e. two consonants) to have the primary stress. Examples (8) to (10) have penultimate stress, while (11), with a complex coda, has final stress. (8) [ˈta.ma] /tama/ tama man 'man' (9) [ˈta.mam] /tamam/ tama=m man=PL 'men' (10) [rai.ˈja.ndun] /rayadun/ ra-ya-dun get-PRES-1DU 'we two are taking' (11) [ku.ˈtɛmr] /kutemr/ kute-m-r cut-PAST2-3SG.M 'he cut' ... Stress can sometimes shift from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable in lists or when calling someone. This latter example is typically heard with kin terms, such as nawa 'mother' ata 'grandmother', etc. Also, the presence of affixes does not affect stress placement; the stressed syllable prior to affixation in verbs, for example (see Chapter 6) retains the stress after tense and person/number/gender marking is added.

new_statements.quote: Most words consist of one or two syllables, the great majority of syllables being V, VC or CV. Some words are tri-syllabic, though this is uncommon. Words longer than three syllables only exist as compound nouns or verbs. Stress is indicated by a higher impressionistic intensity on the stressed vowel. Unstressed vowels are not reduced in any way; they are just not pronounced as prominently as the stressed syllable. Stress in single words almost always falls on the penultimate syllable; there are a few exceptions as detailed in §3.3.1 and §3.3.2. There is also a tendency for words where the final syllable contains a complex coda (i.e. two consonants) to have the primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (simple) word; stress is realised as greater intensity without vowel reduction. Two systematic deviations: (a) words containing the optional [h]/[?] (e.g. kaha 'bad') stress the syllable after that segment, giving final stress in disyllables; (b) a final syllable with a two-consonant coda tends to attract primary stress (ku.'temr 'he cut'). Affixation (tense, person/number/gender) does not shift the stress off the root's stressed syllable. Examples: 'ta.ma 'man', 'ta.mam 'men', rai.'ja.ndun 'we two are taking'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in compounds: in two-word compounds each member keeps its own stress, the second member carrying a weaker secondary stress; in noun-adjective compounds the adjective (second element) has primary stress and the noun weaker stress; in noun-noun compounds each element has full stress; in compounds of four or more syllables primary stress can fall on the antepenult. Sec. 5.11: asymmetric compounds reduce stress on the first noun and enhance it on the second; symmetric compounds give both nouns equal primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with [h]/glottal stop (secs. 3.3.1-3.3.2) stress the following syllable (kaha 'bad' final stress vs kara initial); final syllables with complex codas tend to take primary stress; stress can shift from penult to final syllable in lists or when calling someone (vocative kin terms nawa 'mother', ata 'grandmother'); the dictionary marks irregular stress with ' before the stressed syllable. Some clitics (e.g. ka after the verb) are unstressed, particles carry their own stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('stress in single words'), based on citation and running-text data from Hatfield's fieldwork (2009-2014, NSF-funded); a separate paragraph handles compounds; phrase-level shift noted only for lists and vocatives. Impressionistic (no instrumental study).
new_statements.identity_note: Hatfield 2016 describes spoken Mehek (Glottolog mehe1243, ISO nux) as spoken in the Nuku area villages (main consultants from Kafle and neighbouring villages; a 'Kafle variant' is flagged in the dictionary), treating it as one language with minor village variation. Not to be confused with Mehek Sign Language (mehe1245), which is sec. 9.11 of the same dissertation and where this PDF was first filed today.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Hatfield 2016: stress 'almost always falls on the penultimate syllable') on penultimate primary stress and adds an explicit secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllables/compounds. It does not mention Hatfield's hedges (final stress in some [h]/glottal-stop words; tendency to final stress with complex codas) nor his compound pattern (N-N compounds with full stress on each member); the OPD's blanket 'compound words: penultimate primary, initial secondary' is a coarser statement than Hatfield's sec. 5.11.2 but names the same default placement, so no contradiction in type or default position. Independent, earlier source (Wunum's 1975 Makru phonology ms.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (stated for trisyllabic words and compounds), with a secondary stress on the first syllable. Nothing is said about tone or contrastive length beyond the section heading; no exceptions are listed. Disyllables are not addressed explicitly (penult = initial there, so the statement is consistent with general penultimate stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllabic words and compounds (i.e. initial secondary + penultimate primary)
new_statements.exceptions: none in the OPD (the 'Conventions: Phonological' paragraph concerns allophones of /p/, aspiration of /t k/, and the glottal stop occurring only as onset of the final syllable, e.g. alwaqa 'taro')
new_statements.identity_note: Wunum's OPD describes 'Mehek (Makru)' [NUX], Lumi, Sandaun Province, villages Nuku, Mansuku, Yiminum, Ifkindu, Wilwil, Kafle 1-3 = the Central dialect area of Bugenhagen 1981 (Makru-Klaplei Census Division, Nuku District) and the variety of Hatfield 2016; Bugenhagen distinguishes a Central dialect (Northern sub-dialect chain Ifkindu-Mantsuku-Nuku; Southern sub-dialect Klaplei 1-3, Wilwil) and an Akosamei 1 dialect, with Siliput (Seleput) a separate language.
